issues.legal_issue: An interlocutory order made during a civil proceeding can constitute a case decided for the purpose of revisional jurisdiction.
material_facts: The trial court made an interlocutory order allowing an amendment to the plaint in a pending suit.
The High Court exercised revisional jurisdiction over that order.
issues.conclusion: An interlocutory order can be treated as a case decided and is capable of revision, but the High Court may interfere only within the limits imposed by the proviso to Section 115 CPC.
issues.legal_principle: In Major S.S. Khanna v. Brig. F.J. Dillon, AIR 1964 SC 497, the Court held that “case” in Section 115 CPC includes a part of a civil proceeding and is not confined to the entire proceeding. The 1976 amendment, by adding the explanation to Section 115, adopted that interpretation. The proviso to Section 115 nevertheless restricts interference with interlocutory orders to the specified circumstances.

predicates.civil_proceeding: A civil proceeding is pending before a court.
predicates.subordinate_court_made_interlocutory_ord: A court made an order during the course of that proceeding without finally determining it.

issues.definition: When a court makes an interlocutory order in a civil proceeding, that order counts as a case decided for revision.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not reverse an order allowing amendment of pleadings when the order neither finally disposes of the proceeding nor causes failure of justice or irreparable injury.
material_facts: The trial court allowed the plaintiffs to amend their plaint to plead facts they said they learned from a later suit.
The amendment did not finally dispose of the suit.
The opposing party could respond to the amended pleading, raise defences, and challenge an adverse final decision on appeal.
The High Court set aside the trial court’s order on the ground that the amendment sought to attack an old decree and was time-barred.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in setting aside the order allowing the amendment; the appeal was allowed and the trial court’s order was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under the proviso to Section 115(1) CPC, an interlocutory order may be varied or reversed only if it would finally dispose of the suit or proceeding, or if allowing it to stand would occasion a failure of justice or cause irreparable injury. An order allowing a pleading amendment ordinarily only gives notice of a party’s plea; it does not decide the issues, and the opposing party can answer the amendment and pursue available appellate remedies. The Court held that the amendment order in this case met neither exception.

rule.if: high_court_revision_of_interlocutory_order and order_allows_pleading_amendment and amendment_does_not_end_proceeding and amendment_only_gives_notice_of_a_plea and opponent_can_answer_and_raise_defences and later_appeal_available

predicates.high_court_revision_of_interlocutory_ord: A party asks a High Court to revise an interlocutory order made in a lower court proceeding.
predicates.order_allows_pleading_amendment: The lower court permits a party to amend a pleading.
predicates.amendment_does_not_end_proceeding: Allowing the amendment does not finally dispose of the proceeding.
predicates.amendment_only_gives_notice_of_a_plea: The amendment gives notice of a position the party may take but does not itself decide the disputed issues.
predicates.opponent_can_answer_and_raise_defences: The opposing party has an opportunity to respond to the amended pleading and present defences.
predicates.later_appeal_available: The opposing party can challenge an adverse final decision through an appeal.

issues.definition: If a High Court is asked to revise an interlocutory order allowing a pleading amendment that does not end the proceeding, merely gives notice of a plea, and can be answered and challenged on appeal, revision to reverse that order is not permitted.
